'''''Alternanthera brasiliana''''', also known as '''large purple alternanthera''', '''metal weed''', '''bloodleaf''', '''parrot leaf''', '''ruby leaf''', '''Brazilian joyweed''', '''purple alternanthera''', '''purple joyweed''', is a [[flowering plant]] of the [[amaranth]] family that is native to the forests of [[South America]] and as well as [[Central America]], ranging from northeastern Mexico to northeastern Argentina.<ref name= tropical/><ref name = powo/> It is grown as an [[ornamental plant]].<ref name= brasiliana/>

[[Alternanthera brasiliana var. villosa|''Alternanthera brasiliana'' var. ''villosa'']], a variety known as little ruby or ruby leaf alternanthera, is also known by the [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] ''Alternanthera dentata''.<ref name= brasiliana/><ref name = villosa>[https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:10302-2 ''Alternanthera brasiliana'' var. ''villosa'' (Moq.) Kuntze]. ''[[Plants of the World Online]]''. Retrieved 4 April 2024.</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Alternanthera brasiliana.jpg|thumb|left|Flowers]]
It is an erect, [[groundcover|sprawling]], [[herbaceous plant]] that may grow up to 3 metres tall, though it is usually less than 1 metre as a cultivated plant. The plant's stems, which range between red, green and purple, are delicately hirsute when juvenile, though they'd become glabrescent as they get older. Its [[Opposite (leaf)|opposite leaves]], which are 1–10 cm long and 0.7–5 cm wide, are usually coloured purple-specked or luminous reddish-purple.<ref name= tropical>[http://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Alternanthera+brasiliana Alternanthera brasiliana]</ref> It may lose some of its leaves in winter, making it partially "[[deciduous]]" in places that have slightly cool winters.

Its vanilla-coloured, pom-pom flowers are ordered in compact clusters (7–20 mm long) in the top leaf [[branch]]ing and are small in shape. These clusters are rounded to slightly lengthened in shape and are foaled on [[Petiole (botany)|stalks]] which are normally 3–10 cm long. It can flower any time of the year, but in [[temperate climate|temperate]] and cooler [[subtropical]] climates it flowers more often in winter.<ref>[https://www.news-mail.com.au/news/purple-weed-brings-no-joy/2672166/ Purple weed is a monster] by News Mail, Ian Read, 23rd Jun 2015</ref> Its very small brown fruit (1.5–2 mm long) contains one seed that's generally hidden within the older flower parts.<ref>[https://weeds.brisbane.qld.gov.au/weeds/purple-joyweed Purple joyweed Alternanthera brasiliana]</ref>

==Varieties==
Two varieties are accepted.<ref name = powo/>
*''Alternanthera brasiliana'' var. ''brasiliana'' – northeastern Mexico to central Brazil
*[[Alternanthera brasiliana var. villosa|''Alternanthera brasiliana'' var. ''villosa'']] {{small|(Moq.) Kuntze}} - southeastern Mexico to northeastern Argentina.<ref name = villosa/>

==Cultivation==
It is used as an ornamental plant with many [[cultivars]], such as 'Purple Prince' and 'Little Ruby' (used for the [[Alternanthera brasiliana var. villosa|''Alternanthera brasiliana'' var. ''villosa'']] cultivars). It is often harvested from the wild for regional use as a food and medicine, where it is used as an [[antiviral]] and anti-diarrhoea agent. It grows in full sun in moist, well drained soils, where it will multiply by self-seeding. It can also be easily propagated by [[cuttings (plants)|cuttings]].<ref name= tropical/>

==Range==
The plant is native to [[Brazil]], [[Peru]], [[Ecuador]], [[Colombia]], [[Venezuela]], the [[Guyanas]], [[Nicaragua]], [[Belize]], [[Guatemala]], [[Mexico]], northeastern [[Argentina]], [[Trinidad and Tobago]], [[Aruba]], and the [[Windward Islands]].<ref name = powo/>

Moreover, it is naturalised in the wilderness and cultivated land in [[west Africa]], coastal districts of northern and eastern [[Australia]], [[Florida]], [[South Africa]], some of the [[Pacific Islands]], and in shaded ravine slopes and creeks in [[Java]].<ref name= tropical/> Most species of joyweed, including this one, are considered as [[environmental weed]]s in Queensland, New South Wales, the Northern Territory, and Western Australia.<ref name= brasiliana/>
